question: What is the basic structural and functional unit of the human body?
explanation: The cell is universally recognized as the smallest independent unit capable of carrying out life processes. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h1)

question: Why is it important for nurses to understand basic cell biology?

options.A: It helps calculate precise intravenous drug dosages
options.B: Cell structures instantly tell you a patient's blood type
options.C: Most diseases actually start at the cellular level
options.D: Nurses must examine tissues under a microscope daily

explanation: You've got this! Illness usually begins when individual cells get injured or don't work right, which later affects the whole organ and body. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h1)

question: Where do all brand new cells in the human body come from?
explanation: Think of it like a family tree—cells can only come from older, pre-existing cells dividing to make new ones! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h2)

question: Which everyday body process relies directly on cells dividing to make new ones?
explanation: When you get a cut or scrape, your existing cells have to copy themselves to close the wound and fix your skin. Amazing, right? [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h2)

question: Which part of the cell acts as the main control center and holds our DNA?
explanation: The nucleus is like the brain or command center of the cell, storing all the genetic instructions needed to run the show. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h3)

question: What is the main job of the plasma membrane?

options.B: Digesting cellular waste and foreign invaders
options.C: Controlling what goes in and out of the cell
options.D: Generating chemical energy for cellular work

explanation: The membrane acts like a smart security guard, letting helpful nutrients in and keeping harmful stuff out to keep the cell stable. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h3)

question: Which tiny part inside the cell is famously known as the "powerhouse of the cell"?
explanation: Mitochondria pump out the energy currency (ATP) that your cells need to do all their hard work! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h4)

question: If a cell does a lot of heavy physical work, like a muscle cell, which organelle will it have lots of?
explanation: Hard-working tissues need lots of energy, so they pack extra mitochondria to keep up with the heavy workload. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h4)

question: What is the final result when a normal body cell goes through mitosis?

options.C: A single giant cell with multiple nuclei

explanation: Mitosis is neat and tidy: one cell splits down the middle to create two exact copies for growth and repair. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h5)

question: What usually happens when the body's cell division cycle spins completely out of control?
explanation: When cells lose their normal stop-and-go signals, they keep multiplying wildly, which can form a tumor. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h5)

question: What happens to red blood cells if you drop them into a very watery (hypotonic) solution?
explanation: Because there's more water outside, water rushes into the cell trying to balance things out, making it swell until it pops! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h6)

question: How do many common antibiotics cure an infection without hurting our own human cells?

options.A: They target unique germ structures like cell walls that humans don't have
options.B: They destroy all circulating white blood cells
options.C: They block nerve impulses throughout the body
options.D: They raise the patient's overall body temperature

explanation: This is called selective toxicity! The drug attacks parts of the bacteria that our human cells simply don't have, keeping us safe. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h6)
